title: The cat
hookLine: when I play with my cat, who knows if she is playing with me? (Essays 2.12)

cards: A piece of string dragged slowly across the floor. Under the chair, a cat goes flat, tail twitching. She wiggles, pounces, misses, and looks up at you as if to say that was on purpose.
You're the one holding the string, so you're the one running the game. Aren't you? Montaigne had a cat, and somewhere in the same long essay as yesterday's motto, he stops to ask exactly that.

teach.b: First, the question. When I play with my cat, Montaigne writes, who knows whether she isn't amusing herself with me more than I am with her? It's a light line, and it flips the whole scene.
Maybe you're the toy. Second, the silence between us. People and animals don't fully understand each other, he says, and we assume the failure is theirs.
But why not ours as much as theirs?
It's anybody's guess whose fault it is. By the same reasoning, he adds, they might think of us as the dumb animals.
Third, the dog at the crossroads. He passes along a story from the ancient philosopher Chrysippus. A dog, following its master's trail, comes to a place where three roads meet.
It sniffs a second. Then it runs down the third without sniffing at all, as if it had worked it out: not this one, not that one, so this. Montaigne doesn't wave the story away.
He asks why we're so sure the dog wasn't thinking. Fourth, the point underneath. All of this sits in a long argument against human presumption.
We're fragile, exposed creatures, he says, and at the same time the proudest, and we hand ourselves the top spot without much evidence.
The cat is a gentle example: yesterday's question, what do I know, turned toward the creature on the rug.
Who's playing whom is a good question for a pet, and not a bad one for a toddler, a teenager, or a boss.

how: Readers of Montaigne often remember the cat as a small lesson in humility: when we can't understand another creature, the gap may be ours as much as theirs.

o: Montaigne's cat, who may be playing with him as he with her
a symbol of the soul's freedom in old French poems
his proof that animals can't reason the way we can

p: the gap between us and animals

s: he asks why the failure to understand should be theirs rather than ours.
he suggests animals might think of us as the dumb ones
by the same reasoning, he says, they might take us for beasts.
Montaigne uses his cat to prove that people rule over animals
he uses her to ask the opposite: who knows whether she's amusing herself with him more than he is with her?

games.q: you're a dog, tracking your master, and the trail reaches a place where three roads meet. what does the dog in Montaigne's story do?
o: sits down and waits to be found.
sniffs two roads, then runs down the third without sniffing.
games.why: the story, from Chrysippus, has the dog skip the sniffing on the third road, as if it had reasoned: not this, not that, so this.

practice: If there's an animal near you, a cat, a dog, a bird on a wire, let it be without calling it, and watch where its attention goes, and whether, for a moment, it lands on you.
If there's no animal near, remember how one once looked at you. Ask Montaigne's question quietly, what might I look like from there, and rest in not knowing.

wordCard.voice: The cat. Montaigne, playing with his cat, wonders whether she's playing with him, and asks why the gap between us and animals must be their fault. Today's word.

orig.s: quand je me joue à ma chatte
orig.say: kahn zhuh muh ZHOO ah mah SHAHT
orig.note: French, from the Apology for Raymond Sebond: when I play with my cat.

carryVoice: Your line: who's playing whom. The cat may have her own view of the game. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Essays 2.12, Apology for Raymond Sebond (when I play with my cat, who knows whether she makes me her pastime more than I make her mine; the defect in communication may be ours as much as theirs; animals may take us for beasts; Chrysippus's dog at the meeting of three roads; presumption as our natural malady)
